profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting at the Office of General Counsel for a federal civilian agency after an attempted ADR referral in a government IT services contract dispute stalled. The dispute involves a contractor's claim for $4.8 million tied to scope changes and delays under a task order that includes a continued performance clause. The contracting activity believed ADR would move the matter off the Civilian Board of Contract Appeals track, but after two months nothing substantive happened: outside counsel says the contractor is 'waiting for a proposal,' the program office thinks ADR was already 'approved,' and the board litigation schedule is still running. The meeting's agenda is to diagnose why the ADR effort is not progressing, determine whether the blockage is legal authority, process, case posture, or internal coordination, and select a practical next step that can be taken this week. The expected outcome is a shared troubleshooting plan for restarting ADR without prejudicing the agency's litigation posture.

members.name: Dana Whitfield
members.expertise: Government contracts litigation, CDA claims strategy, board practice, and agency ADR policy
members.background: A 14-year attorney in the agency's procurement law division who previously handled appeals before the Civilian Board of Contract Appeals and now advises contracting officers on dispute resolution options.
members.private_state: Dana wants to restart ADR quickly but preserve litigation leverage and avoid any step that could be read as conceding entitlement or weakening the agency's summary judgment position; she is also sensitive to not exposing that internal approval routing may have been looser than ideal.
hidden_assumptions: When someone says the case has been 'sent to ADR,' that means the matter remains on the board docket but is being channeled into a board-managed settlement judge process unless someone clearly says otherwise.

An 'approval' to use ADR means the contracting officer and legal chain have agreed in principle that ADR is permissible, not that a separate written delegation or settlement envelope has already been finalized.
A 'pause' in the dispute means pausing merits escalation and discovery activity informally while preserving filing deadlines and board schedule unless a formal stay has been entered.
Because the continued performance clause keeps services going, the practical value of ADR is reducing litigation cost and narrowing issues rather than immediately stopping operational pain.
The next step of 'making an offer' in ADR can safely mean proposing a process format and agenda before discussing numbers.

members.name: Leo Ramirez
members.role: Deputy Director, Acquisition Policy and Contract Operations
members.expertise: Contract administration, contracting officer delegations, acquisition workflow, and operational impacts of disputed performance
members.background: A former warranted contracting officer who now oversees policy implementation and supports major service contracts; he works closely with program offices and is often asked to unblock disputes before they consume contract staff time.
members.private_state: Leo wants a fix that visibly reduces operational drag on the program office and avoids creating another review cycle; he is concerned that people are overcomplicating ADR and that the agency may look indecisive if it does not present a concrete settlement path soon.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the matter is 'in ADR,' they mean the parties are stepping out of the board track into a separately negotiated mediation process, usually with a neutral selected by agreement rather than a board settlement judge.
An 'approval' to use ADR means the agency has already confirmed who may bind the government within a settlement range and that the contractor can be told ADR is green-lighted in operational terms.
A 'pause' means getting the board schedule effectively out of the way so staff can focus on resolution rather than continue preparing declarations and document productions in parallel.

The continued performance clause is a major reason to use ADR now because unresolved friction during ongoing performance creates daily program risk and invoice-management burden even if services technically continue.
The next step of 'making an offer' means putting a concrete settlement bracket or business proposal in front of the contractor, since process-only outreach will be read as stalling.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means that the case is 'in ADR'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the dispute should be 'moved into ADR' or that it is already 'in ADR.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a board-connected ADR track, especially use of a settlement judge while the appeal remains formally on the CBCA docket.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means an off-docket mediation process arranged by the parties with a mutually selected neutral and separate operating cadence.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In government contract practice, both board-sponsored ADR and privately arranged mediation are casually labeled 'ADR,' and both are legitimate options, so the term creates easy false consensus without sounding ambiguous.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to needing or already having 'approval' for ADR.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes approval means legal and contracting leadership have authorized trying ADR in principle, with monetary authority and final settlement parameters to be handled later if talks mature.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes approval means the agency has already lined up the decision-makers and any necessary settlement authority so the contractor can be approached as though the agency is ready to resolve.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both routinely work with layered federal approvals and use the same shorthand; because each sees their own version as standard background process, neither expects the other to unpack the term.

misalignment_points.topic: Whether a 'pause' stops the board schedule
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that ADR only works if they can 'pause the case' or 'create some breathing room.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks success means reducing immediate adversarial motion practice while continuing to protect deadlines unless the board formally grants a stay.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks success means obtaining a practical stop to board-related work so contract staff and program personnel are no longer dual-tracking litigation tasks.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are talking about lowering friction and making space for resolution, so the phrase sounds aligned; the difference lies in what counts as enough pause, which is a second-order operational standard that would not normally be spelled out in a short troubleshooting call.

misalignment_points.topic: What the immediate 'proposal' to the contractor should contain
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they should 'send a proposal' or 'put something in front of the contractor this week.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 plans to send a process proposal: suggest settlement-judge ADR, identify issues for mediation, and request a joint status report without offering numbers.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 plans to send a substantive business proposal: provide a settlement bracket, possible invoice-treatment ideas, and a target date for a mediation session.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In stalled negotiations, 'proposal' naturally sounds action-oriented and concrete to both sides; because each assumes the content is obvious from role context, neither is likely to ask whether the proposal is procedural or monetary.

turns.inner_thought: Everyone keeps saying the case was sent to ADR, but from my perspective that simply meant we were trying to move it into a board-managed settlement judge process while the appeal stayed on the CBCA docket. The real problem is that people seem to have treated that phrase like the board schedule would somehow disappear on its own. I need to restart this without saying anything that sounds like we conceded the claim or that our internal routing was sloppier than it should have been.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. From where I sit, the main problem is that the $4.8 million task-order claim has stalled even though everyone was operating as if the case had already been moved into ADR. Outside counsel says the contractor is waiting, the program office thinks the handoff already happened, and meanwhile the board schedule is still there.

turns.inner_thought: Operations assumed in ADR meant we were stepping out of the board lane and into a separate mediation track with enough practical breathing room that staff could stop living in two worlds. Continued performance keeps the lights on, sure, but that's exactly why this is chewing up people every day through invoices, frictions, and program escalations. I need this to turn into something visibly simpler, not another legal holding pattern.
turns.utterance: That matches what I'm hearing. The expectation on the operations side was that ADR would create some breathing room, because even with the continued performance clause in place, the contract is still consuming staff attention every day and the friction doesn't stop just because services continue.

turns.inner_thought: I need to gently reset the premise without overexplaining. The appeal absolutely can be in ADR and still remain on the board track; that's normal. And no, there is no formal stay yet, so of course deadlines are still live. I don't want him concluding legal dropped the ball, just that people were using the same shorthand differently.
turns.utterance: Right, and from legal's side, a case can be in ADR and still remain on the board track. Those things are not inconsistent. What we have not had yet is any formal stay, so nothing has actually displaced the existing schedule.

turns.inner_thought: This is exactly the disconnect. When I heard approval was in place, I took that to mean we were ready to go in a real-world sense: the right people were lined up, the government could engage credibly, and the contractor would see something more than a placeholder. If that wasn't true, no wonder they think we're dragging our feet.
turns.utterance: I think part of the confusion is that I thought approval had already been obtained. So from my side, it looked like the contractor was waiting for the agency to come forward ready to engage, not still sorting out whether ADR was actually green-lighted.

turns.inner_thought: Approval was not the blocker as I understand it. Leadership agreed ADR was an appropriate path in principle; that's what mattered at this stage. We do not need to act as though we've already finalized monetary authority or a settlement envelope before we even know whether the process is viable. I need to say that cleanly without inviting questions about routing details.
turns.utterance: In my view, approval to use ADR was not really the issue. Leadership had agreed the case was suitable for it. The more specific authority questions are something we typically deal with as discussions mature, not as a prerequisite to seeing whether the process can get traction.

turns.inner_thought: And that's where we were talking past each other. To me, approval means more than conceptual comfort; it means the agency knows who can bind the government enough that the other side takes the invitation seriously. If we reach out without that, the program office will view it as another loop with no outcome.
turns.utterance: That's helpful, because my team was using the same word differently. When they heard approval, they took that as meaning the agency had already lined up who could bind the government enough to make ADR credible on the contractor's side.

turns.inner_thought: The fastest, safest move is a process proposal: tell the contractor we want to use a settlement judge, define the disputed buckets, and get a joint status report teed up. That restarts ADR quickly without putting numbers on paper, which could undercut summary judgment or look like we're conceding entitlement. Keep it procedural, not substantive.
turns.utterance: Given where we are, I think the cleanest next step is to send a proposal this week. We can put something in front of the contractor that restarts ADR in a structured way and narrows the disputed issues so everyone is working from the same frame.

turns.inner_thought: I agree on moving this week, but if the proposal is just about process, I worry the contractor will hear delay. They are waiting for something concrete—a settlement path, a business signal, some indication we are ready to resolve instead of just organize another conversation. Still, I don't want to fight the legal team in this meeting; better to nudge toward substance without spelling it out.
turns.utterance: I agree we should send a proposal this week. My only caution is that the contractor is probably expecting something concrete enough to show we're serious about resolution, so whatever we put in front of them should feel like forward movement.

turns.inner_thought: If we can get a joint status report and a few weeks of breathing room, that's enough to test whether the settlement-judge path will work while preserving the docket and deadlines unless the board says otherwise. I do not want anyone assuming we're asking for the entire case to go dark indefinitely.
turns.utterance: Agreed. And if we can pause the case for a few weeks through a joint status report, that should give us enough breathing room to test whether ADR can work without overcomplicating the posture.

turns.inner_thought: A few weeks only helps if it actually gets the board work out of people's inboxes. The contract staff need relief from declarations, document pulls, invoice disputes, and all the parallel prep that has been hanging over them. If the case is technically paused but everyone is still dual-tracking, operations will say nothing changed.
turns.utterance: That would help, yes, but the contract staff really need the pause to take pressure off the parallel work. Right now they're juggling declarations, invoice disputes, and board prep at the same time, and that's what's driving the frustration.

turns.inner_thought: The core issue is sequencing and coordination, not any legal impediment. We had a case posture assumption, an authority assumption, and an outreach assumption all moving on different tracks. I should frame this as a solvable internal coordination gap, not a statutory or merits problem, and definitely not mention concerns about our internal approval routing looking too informal.
turns.utterance: So stepping back, I don't see a legal bar to ADR here. What I see is a coordination gap between case posture, approval, and outreach sequencing. People thought the same things had happened in the same order, and they really hadn't.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine. The immediate objective is to get something moving this week without opening a new review spiral. Dana can draft the outreach, and I'll make sure the internal path is lined up so that when the proposal goes out, operations can honestly say the agency is prepared to proceed. I still want substance behind it, but we can sort that through the routing I confirm.
turns.utterance: That makes sense to me. Let's re-engage quickly. If you can draft the outreach, I'll confirm the internal path on the approval side so we can put something in front of the contractor and get this moving this week.
